results.C3_head_to_head: None with a discrimination metric: no classifier, AUC or accuracy is computed. The within-study, same-participant comparison uses group tests only (Wilcoxon rank-sum; BH-FDR within each band across 19 electrodes for PSD, sample entropy and nodal efficiency). Direction: complexity (multiscale sample entropy at C4), wPLI connectivity and graph measures separated MCI from HC, and PSD did not. The difference between domains is not itself tested.
results.dataset_family: Hanyang University Hospital outpatient memory clinic, Department of Neurology (Seoul and Guri, Korea); 12 MCI (Petersen criteria) / 13 HC
results.method_family: 19-channel eyes-closed rsEEG (100 s artifact-free); multitaper PSD in 5 bands; multiscale sample and permutation entropy; wPLI functional connectivity; binary graph metrics (global, local and nodal efficiency; small-world sigma) across sparsity thresholds; Wilcoxon rank-sum with BH-FDR; no classifier
results.why: C1 yes. Sample entropy at C4 (scale 4), wPLI in delta/theta/beta/gamma electrode pairs and theta nodal efficiency at Fz and Fp2 differ between MCI and HC after FDR. Global efficiency (theta, alpha, gamma), local efficiency (gamma) and beta small-worldness also differ, in narrow sparsity windows. C2 yes. Band power showed no MCI-HC difference in any band or channel after the same per-band, 19-electrode FDR procedure that sample entropy and nodal efficiency survived, so at the electrode level the comparison is like for like. Caveats: n = 25. The complexity result is one channel at one scale, and permutation entropy was null. The methods exclude network efficiency and small-world from FDR, while the captions of Figs 5 and 7 say FDR-corrected, so the correction status of those results is internally inconsistent. K-MMSE differs between groups (p = 0.02) but CDR-SB does not. The authors flag low power. C4 not tested: the domains are never combined.

quotes.quote: The results revealed no significant difference in EEG spectral power between the HC and MCI groups. However, we observed significant changes in brain complexity and networks in individuals with MCI compared with HC.
This study aimed to compare the effectiveness of MCI diagnosis by investigating differences in PSD, complexity, functional connectivity, and graph analysis between individuals with MCI and HCs.

We also adjusted the p-values for PSD, complexity, functional connectivity, and nodal efficiency using a false discovery rate (FDR) test to control for multiple comparisons excluding network efficiency and small world.
For the analyses of PSD, complexity, and nodal efficiency, the FDR approach was applied separately within each frequency band across all nineteen electrodes.
However, no significant differences were found between the HC and MCI groups in any of the frequency bands and channels after FDR correction.
Consequently, in the C4 channel, there was a statistically significant difference between the two groups (p=0.0019, pFDR = 0.037) (Figure 3C).
however, no significant difference was found between the HC and MCI groups across all channels (Figure 3D).
Significant differences were observed in wPLI values between the MCI and HC groups for all frequency bands except the alpha band (Figure 4).
In the theta band, we observed a significant difference in the global efficiency between the two groups when the sparsity threshold was varied from 12% to 25%.

the HC group showed higher node efficiency in the frontal region, Fz (p = 0.004, pFDR = 0.039) and Fp2 (p = 0.002, pFDR = 0.039), than the MCI group, with the threshold of 20% being the most statistically significant.
The difference between the MCI and HC groups was statistically significant for small-world networks within a sparsity threshold of 76% to 80% in the beta band.
First, the relatively small sample size of the participants in each group (n = 13 for HC and n = 12 for MCI) might have limited the statistical power of the results of this study.

results.C3_head_to_head: None. Only connectivity-dynamics features are used. No spectral, complexity or other-domain comparator is computed.
results.dataset_family: Wayne State University Institute of Gerontology (Healthier Black Elders Center) and Michigan ADRC (MADRC) community-dwelling Black Americans, Detroit; 84 HC / 53 MCI by MADRC consensus using NACC UDS
results.method_family: 64-channel eyes-closed rsEEG (110 s), CSD over 12 ROIs; multiscale sliding-window Pearson-correlation connectivity with wavelet features; t-test feature screening, regularised LDA, AdaBoost, weighted majority voting of 21 classifiers; LOO and k-fold CV
results.why: C1 yes. A classifier built only from time-varying ROI-to-ROI Pearson-correlation connectivity separates 53 MCI from 84 HC (LOO 91.97%, 3-fold 91.17%). Caveat: features were screened by t-test on all 137 participants before cross-validation, and the 21 voters were chosen by their leave-one-out accuracy, so the accuracies are optimistic (selection leakage). C2 not tested: no band-power measure is computed anywhere in the paper. C4 not tested: the ensemble combines 64 configurations of the same connectivity features (window size x number of features), not different feature domains. Other: the aMCI/naMCI split is 42/11 in the text but 36/17 in Table 1 and p.6. Age differs across groups (p = 0.04). Diagnosis is by MADRC consensus using NACC UDS, but the EEG data are the study's own. Whether other corpus papers from this Wayne State/Michigan group reuse the sample was not checked here.

results.C3_head_to_head: None. No spectral-power or other-domain comparator is computed, and there is no classification.
results.dataset_family: Resting-state MEG from Hokuto Hospital (Obihiro) and Kumagaya General Hospital (Japan), analysed by the University of Valladolid group; 67 HC (37 HCtrain / 30 HCtest) / 44 MCI / 50 AD
results.method_family: 160-channel resting MEG, wMNE source reconstruction over 68 Desikan-Killiany ROIs; orthogonalised amplitude-envelope correlation in 1-Hz bins; Connectivity-based Meta-Bands (Louvain community detection on the HCtrain subset) and derived metrics (TA, AS, DoD, switching rate, band Lempel-Ziv complexity); bootstrap group tests with BH-FDR; no classifier
results.why: C1 yes, with thin reporting. Topological adaptation (TA) differs between HC and MCI in every comparison involving the meta-band-1 connectivity matrices, and so does the standard deviation of the degree of dominance (bootstrap, 50,000 resamples, BH-FDR, p < 0.05). The paper prints no p-values or effect sizes for these comparisons; significance appears only as bars in Figs 3 and 4. The HC comparator in the tests is the 30-person HCtest subset, not all 67 controls. Mean attraction strength, mean DoD, switching rate and band Lempel-Ziv complexity separate only HC from AD, so the complexity-type measure (BLZC) does not separate MCI. HC (71.0 years) and MCI (77.2 years) differ in age; the authors report no age correlation with any parameter. C2 not tested: spectral power is never computed. The paper's critique of fixed frequency bands concerns band segmentation for connectivity, not band-power features. C4 not tested. Whether other Valladolid-group corpus papers reuse the Hokuto/Kumagaya MEG sample was not checked here.

quotes.quote: Furthermore, all the comparisons involving the connectivity matrices assigned to meta-band 1 show statistically significant differences between HC and MCI patients as well.
the standard deviation of the DoD obtains statistically significant differences for the three comparisons under study (HC-MCI, HC-AD, and MCI-AD).
Furthermore, both of them display statistically significant differences between HC and AD patients.
Statistically significant between-group differences are indicated with horizontal grey lines (p < 0.05, bootstraping approach FDR-corrected).
The data distribution of the HCtrain is displayed for completeness, but it is not included in the comparisons.
The HC sample was randomly divided into two different subsets: (i) the HCtrain subset, composed of 37 subjects; and (ii) the HCtest subset, composed of 30 subjects.
Results showed no significant impact in any of the parameters under study (p-value > 0.05, Spearman’s correlation test, FDR corrected).

results.C3_head_to_head: None with a discrimination metric: group tests only (ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis with Bonferroni-corrected post hoc tests); no classifier. For MCI vs HC the printed effect sizes are about equal across domains: relative delta power in the left central ROI d = 0.645, microstate C duration d = 0.65. The authors' conclusion that microstates are 'the most prominent EEG marker' rests on which tests reached significance, not on a tested comparison.
results.dataset_family: PREVIEW prospective cohort, Careggi University Hospital / IRCCS Fondazione Don Carlo Gnocchi, Florence, Italy; 57 SCD / 46 MCI / 19 volunteer HC
results.method_family: 64-channel eyes-closed rsEEG; Welch relative and absolute band power (global and 6 ROIs); eLORETA source imaginary coherence with weighted graph metrics (strength, clustering, path length, small-world omega); EEG microstates (duration, coverage, occurrence, transitions, Lempel-Ziv complexity, Hurst exponent); group tests; no classifier
results.why: C1 partly. Against HC, no connectivity, network or complexity measure is shown to separate MCI. Average strength, clustering and path length do not; small-worldness differs only SCD vs MCI, in delta; LZ complexity differs only SCD vs MCI. For the Hurst exponent the text says SCD and MCI are both closer to a random walk than HC, but the printed post hoc tests are HC vs SCD and SCD vs MCI, with no HC vs MCI value. The one measure that does separate MCI from HC, microstate C duration (p = 0.029), measures microstate temporal dynamics, not connectivity, network structure or complexity. Against SCD, LZ complexity, Hurst exponent and delta small-worldness separate MCI; SCD is a self-referred patient group, not a healthy control. C2 partly, on the SCD comparator only. Band power does not separate SCD from MCI (delta average post hoc p = 0.163; ROI post hoc tests significant only for MCI vs HC), while LZ complexity, Hurst exponent and small-worldness do. Against HC, band power is not null: relative delta in the left central ROI is higher in MCI (p = 0.047, d = 0.645). C4 not tested. Caveats: only 19 HC, younger and more educated than MCI (64.3 vs 74.3 years; 15.6 vs 10.0 years of education); no correction across domains; the authors call the small-worldness difference 'sub-optimal for decoding'.

quotes.quote: Statistically, the differences were significant for the delta band (ANOVA F-statistic = 3.29, p = 0.041, η2 = 0.052), but not in the alpha band (ANOVA F-statistic = 2.24, p = 0.111, η2 = 0.036). Post-hoc testing between group pairs in the delta band did not reveal any significant difference at the average power level (t-test post-hoc, HC vs. SCD: p = 0.707, Cohen’s d = 0.25, HC vs. MCI: p = 0.063, Cohen’s d = 0.64, SCD vs. MCI: p = 0.163, Cohen’s d = 0.385).

Post-hoc comparisons in these two areas revealed a significant increase in the delta power in the left central ROI in the MCI group, when compared to HC (t-test post-hoc: p = 0.047, Cohen’s d = 0.645).
We conclude that, although spectral alterations might be induced by the MCI condition, their reliability is too low to lay the ground for EEG-based early prediction of dementia.

the only one with significant changes among groups was the small-worldness (Fig. 3D) (Kruskal-Wallis H-statistic = 9.548, p = 0.0085). Interestingly, SCD small-worldness resulted significantly higher compared to MCI (Wilcoxon post-hoc: p = 0.012, Cohen’s d = 0.56) but not to HC (Wilcoxon post-hoc: p = 0.119, Cohen’s d = 0.63).

Post-hoc testing revealed that microstate C displayed a decreased duration and coverage in MCI compared to HC (Wilcoxon post-hoc, duration: p = 0.029, Cohen’s d = 0. 65, coverage: p = 0.080, Cohen’s d = 0.73)

the structure of the temporal patterns of microstates was significantly altered in MCI, as indicated by a decrease in the LZ complexity compared to SCD (see section 2.6, Fig. 4F, left): Kruskal-Wallis H-statistic = 9.02, p = 0.011, post-hoc SCD vs MCI: p = 0.026, Cohen’s d = 0.45).

Moreover, the long-term memory measured through the Hurst exponent (see section 2.6 for details) resulted in microstate patterns closer to a random walk, both in SCD and MCI compared to HC (Kruskal-Wallis H-statistic = 11.05, p = 0.0040, post-hoc HC vs SCD: p = 0.018, Cohen’s d = 0.63; SCD vs MCI: p = 0.002 8, Cohen’s d = 0.87; Fig. 3F, right).
This u-shaped difference deserves further investigation but might be sub-optimal for decoding the patient’s clinical condition.
In conclusion, microstate analysis revealed to be the most prominent EEG marker to distinguish SCD, MCI and controls.

results.C3_head_to_head: None. The only classifier is a preliminary SVM on regional partial coherence (eyes closed, all bands; 10-fold CV, balanced groups) with 70% accuracy and no band-power or other-domain comparator. The within-study cross-domain contrast is a significant group test (local PCOH cluster test) against a non-significant one (band-averaged PSD), not a tested difference.
results.dataset_family: ALBION (Aiginition Longitudinal Biomarker Investigation Of Neurodegeneration), Cognitive Disorders Clinic, Aiginition Hospital, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens; 21 amnestic MCI / 62 CN, both stable over two yearly evaluations
results.method_family: 19-channel rsEEG (eyes closed and eyes open); VAR-based ordinary coherence and partial coherence up to 100 Hz (pairwise, global, local, post hoc central-regional); Welch t-tests, BY-FDR and cluster-based permutation tests; Welch PSD band averages as a descriptive comparator; preliminary SVM only
results.why: C1 yes. Local partial coherence is higher in aMCI in cluster-based permutation tests (eyes closed, 32-100 Hz, p = 0.0290; eyes open, 28-100 Hz, p = 0.0272). Regional central PCOH in gamma gives p = 0.012-0.017 (d = 0.76-0.82), but that region was chosen from the cluster results. Ordinary coherence is null at global, local and cluster level (eyes-open cluster p = 0.085). Global PCOH is null, and pairwise and per-electrode tests do not survive FDR (minimum adjusted p 0.058 and 0.1429). C2 partly. Band-averaged PSD 'did not indicate any significant difference' while local PCOH did, which is the clause's pattern. But the PSD analysis is one sentence with no test, level or statistic. PSD got no cluster test, while connectivity was tested at four levels. At the matched whole-head level, connectivity was also null. Descriptively, MCI had higher high-frequency power, in the same direction as the gamma PCOH effect. C4 not tested. The logistic model mentioned in the limitations combines regional PCOH with demographics and cognitive scores, not spectral features, and reports no numbers. Other: the groups differ in age (p = 0.001) and education (p < 0.001), and adjustment reportedly did not change the results. There is no amyloid or tau confirmation, the reference is near Fpz, and eye blinks were not removed. Registry defects from round 21 still stand: Sample_N_Approx reads 21 and Dataset 'not reported', whereas N = 83 and the dataset is ALBION.

quotes.quote: Since the connectivity analysis is in the frequency domain, we also use power spectral density to explore the frequency content of the EEG signals.

Comparing between subject groups, it seems that the MCI group has somewhat higher power at the higher frequency bands, especially for the eyes open condition (Fig. 1(b)). The same are more clearly observed in the average PSD (Fig. 1(c-d)). Statistical analysis of the PSD averaged in each band did not indicate any significant difference.
if we correct for multiple comparisons no p-value survives even at a = 0.05. FDR correction of the p-values with produced adjusted p-values that were at minimum 0.058.
For all metrics and frequency bands the results showed that there is no statistically significant difference between the two groups at a = 0.05.
The above statistical results, unfortunately, do not survive FDR correction (smallest corrected p-value was 0.1429).
The p-value of this cluster is 0.085 indicating no statistically significant difference.

For lPEC (Fig. 9c) there is one cluster corresponding to 32 to 100 Hz and channels C3, P3, O1, P4, Fz, Cz, Pz, for which local connectivity is statistically significant different between the MCI and CN subjects (p = 0.0290) and shows higher connectivity for the MCI subjects. Lastly, for lPEO (Fig. 9d) the cluster is in the range 28 to 100 Hz (covering the whole γ band), includes channels C3, P3, P4, Fz, Cz and Pz (very similar to those of lPEC) with a p-value of p = 0.0272, and again shows higher local connectivity for the MCI group.

Based on our observations from the analysis at the global and local level we define a constrained version of global connectivity, which we term as regional connectivity and where we average only the pairwise connectivities inside a given region.
The smallest p-values are, again, obtained for the two γ bands with p = 0.017 and p = 0.015 for rPEC and p = 0.014 and p = 0.012 for rPEO.
Most of the observed differences were statistically significant only for partial coherence but not for ordinary coherence.

This study is purely statistical and does not investigate the actual predictive or prognostic capabilities of the metrics. In the future we plan to explicitly address this. A preliminary classification study with support vector machines (with 10-fold cross validation and balancing the groups) provided accuracy of 70 % when using regional partial coherence under EC in all bands.

We also attempted predictive modelling using a multiple logistic regression model with input the regional connectivity metrics, demographic information (age, sex, etc.) and cognitive tests scores. The results indicated that the EEG-based partial coherence metrics provided predictive information that is not included in the other variables.

There were statistically significant differences with respect to age (p = 0.001) and education level (p < 0.001), but as mentioned above this did not result in confounding effects for the connectivity analysis.

results.C3_head_to_head: None. No classifier ('since no classification was performed'); group tests only.
results.dataset_family: Tongji Hospital (Tongji University School of Medicine) Department of Neurology / Memory Clinic, Shanghai; single site, recruited January 2018 to December 2021; 43 HC / 46 MCI / 43 AD
results.method_family: 64-channel eyes-closed rsEEG; within-electrode phase-amplitude coupling (Tort modulation index, 10 band pairs) averaged globally and over 8 regions; Welch relative band power as a prerequisite check; Kruskal-Wallis with FDR over regions and DSCF post hoc tests; no classifier
results.why: C1 partly, and only if within-region phase-amplitude coupling counts as a connectivity-class measure. PAC is computed per electrode and averaged within regions ('our study only measured CFC in the same brain areas'), so it is not inter-regional connectivity, a graph metric or a signal-complexity measure. On that broad reading, region-level PAC separates MCI from HC in four region-by-pair cells: delta-gamma right temporal p = 0.022 and right parietal p = 0.005; theta-gamma right temporal p = 0.049 and right parietal p = 0.029 (DSCF post hoc after FDR-corrected Kruskal-Wallis). The 'right temporal' region is a single electrode (T8). Global PAC does not separate HC from MCI. C2 partly. Relative band power differs only for AD (theta up and gamma down vs both HC and MCI). No HC-MCI power statistic is printed; the discussion states an 'absence of abnormal power in MCI patients'. The contrast is whole-head power against region-level coupling: at the matched whole-head level coupling was also null for HC vs MCI, and power was never analysed by region. C4 not tested. Other: MCI was diagnosed clinically, with no amyloid or tau confirmation. Table 2's MCI-AD and HC-AD columns appear swapped relative to the text; the HC-MCI column is non-significant throughout. The groups are matched on age, sex and education.

quotes.quote: we investigated the PAC mode by computing the MI between the low-frequency phase and the high-frequency amplitude for each electrode.
left temporal (T7), right temporal (T8)

As noted by Aru et al. (2015), a clear peak in the power spectrum of the low frequency component is a prerequisite for a meaningful interpretation of any CFC pattern. So before performing the CFC analysis, we calculated the Welch’s power

Specifically, the relative power of low-frequency theta oscillations in AD patients was significantly higher than that in HC (p = 0.008) and MCI (p = 0.006). Also, the relative power of high-frequency gamma oscillations in AD patients was significantly lower than that in HC (p < 0.001) and MCI (p < 0.001).
Furthermore, there was no discernible difference in the strength of the global-level coupling in the HC and MCI groups.

while only delta-gamma coupling in the right temporal lobe (p = 0.022) and the parietal lobe (p = 0.005) and theta-gamma coupling in the right temporal lobe (p = 0.049) and the parietal lobe (p = 0.029) showed significant variations between HCs and MCI patients.
the abnormal gamma oscillations power in AD patients and the absence of abnormal power in MCI patients observed in this study may reflect a possible compensatory mechanism early in the onset of AD
P-values are FDR-corrected for Kruskal–Wallis test. The post hoc P-values are DSCF-corrected for multiple comparisons between groups

And since no classification was performed, we do not know whether the coupling features described here effectively distinguish among different groups of subjects; this point can be addressed in future work.
This suggests that future studies should further investigate this type of coupling since our study only measured CFC in the same brain areas.

clause_tally.C1: yes: P-553 (Hanyang), P-501 (Wayne State/MADRC), P-463 (Hokuto/Kumagaya MEG), P-368 (ALBION), four distinct dataset families. partly: P-480 (only against SCD; no in-class measure separates MCI from HC), P-552 (only if within-region PAC is counted in the class).
clause_tally.C2: yes: P-553 only. partly: P-368 (PSD null reported without statistics and not analysed at the level where connectivity separated), P-552 (whole-head power against region-level PAC; no HC-MCI power statistic printed), P-480 (holds against SCD only; against HC, left-central delta power also separates). not_tested: P-501, P-463.
clause_tally.C3: No current supporter runs a within-study, same-participant head-to-head of a discrimination metric between feature domains. P-553, P-480, P-368 and P-552 contrast domains only as significant against non-significant group tests; P-480's printed MCI-HC effect sizes are equal across domains (d = 0.645 vs 0.65). The classifiers in P-501 and P-368 are single-domain.
clause_tally.C4: not_tested in all six. No current supporter combines spectral with complexity or connectivity features.
